transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SRE), Michael (BrightScale), Aisha (BrightScale CTO), Danielle (BrightScale Infra), Owen (BrightScale SRE)
---
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Goal for today is a deep dive on throughput tuning for your production workload - continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, kv cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs and VPC considerations.
[00:18] Michael: Thanks. We're mostly focused on peak-hour latency and cost, we had some spikes last quarter when a campaign doubled qps.
[00:25] Samir (Redwood SE): Got it, can you briefly outline your current setup? GPUs, models, and network topology?
[00:33] Danielle: We're on GCP, n1 with A100s right now in a private VPC. Models are a 13B quantized variant, using your hosted API originally but moving to Dedicated in our VPC.
[00:42] Aisha: Main constraint is 99th pct latency < 300ms for short completions, and batch throughput during bulk jobs. Also security: audit logs and KMS keys in our account.
[00:55] Samir: Great. Two high-level levers we tune: server-side scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, continuous batching thresholds) and model-level knobs (kv cache size, quantization profile). We'll walk through them and tradeoffs.
[01:12] Jordan: Quick note - we'll drop a shared spreadsheet and the scheduler knobs doc in the chat after the call.
[01:20] Michael: Cool. Can you explain continuous batching again, I think that's where we lost some headroom?
[01:26] Samir: Sure - continuous batching keeps worker queues open for a short window to aggregate requests, instead of strict per-request scheduling. It reduces per-token overhead and improves GPU utilization. But it increases tail latency if your window or max_num_seqs is too aggressive.
[01:40] Owen: Our traffic is spiky, with short bursts of 50-200 rps for a few minutes. Does continuous batching help?
[01:47] Samir: Yes for bursty workloads it often helps - you can set the batching window to something like 8-15ms and increase max_num_seqs so we can pack multiple short inferences into one micro-batch. But if most requests are single-token or need <100ms end-to-end, too large a window hurts.
[02:04] Danielle: What's the default max_num_seqs you recommend for 13B models?
[02:09] Samir: Default in our Dedicated runtime is 8 for latency-first profiles, 16-32 for throughput profiles. For your A100s and 13B quantized, we usually start with 16 and tune from there.
[02:20] Michael: And how do token limits interact? We have inputs varying 8-400 tokens.
[02:26] Priya (Redwood SRE): Important: batching packs sequences, not tokens. If you have many long sequences the effective batch size becomes smaller. We recommend capping request tokens to avoid OOMs on KV cache during heavy batches - e.g., set per-request max_input_tokens=512 and enforce token throttles at the edge.
[02:42] Aisha: We were considering no token caps to be flexible for customers - is that risky?
[02:47] Samir: It is. Uncapped long requests cause kv cache growth and can evict others or force smaller micro-batches; worst-case you get poor GPU utilization and higher p99 latency. If you need flexibility, use adaptive admission: accept long requests but throttle them during peak windows or route to a separate node pool.
[03:05] Michael: How do you measure kv cache hit rate? Our engineers say they see low reuse.
[03:10] Priya: KV cache reuse depends on prompt prefixes and conversation continuity. For chat-like workflows you get high reuse. For one-off single-shot prompts reuse is low. We instrument per-route kv_cache_hit_rate and tokenize prefix lengths in the console; Samir will share the query for our dashboard.
[03:26] Samir: Also note our runtime supports prefix caching and shared prefix caches for identical context across requests, which increases effective batching efficiency.
[03:33] Danielle: On quantization - we saw slight QA regressions when moving from 4-bit to 8-bit configurations, any suggestions?
[03:40] Samir: There's a tradeoff: more aggressive quantization (4-bit) reduces memory and increases throughput but can slightly change output distribution. We ship recommended quant profiles per model. For throughput-critical, we usually try q4 and validate with your eval set; for strict quality, q8 or bf16 is better. We'll provide the quantization guidance doc and perf numbers.
[03:58] Michael: Can we run A/B quality tests as part of the pilot?
[04:02] Jordan: Absolutely - we'd run a canary rollout: 5% traffic on q4, monitor eval metrics and regressions, then scale. We also have automatic rollback policies if quality drops.
[04:12] Aisha: Networking - in VPC mode what are the gotchas? We worry about egress and NAT bottlenecks.
[04:18] Priya: In Private deployments we recommend colocating inference nodes in the same subnet and using internal load balancing. Avoid centralized NAT for high qps; NAT gateways can saturate. Also ensure MTU settings match between your environment and the data plane.
[04:32] Owen: Any specifics about port ranges or idle timeouts that trip sessions?
[04:36] Priya: We'll share a checklist. Short version: keep TCP idle timeouts > 120s for long-running streams, open the ephemeral port range we list in the doc, and ensure health check intervals align with autoscaler.
[04:49] Michael: Back to scheduler knobs - you mentioned max_tokens_per_batch too?
[04:54] Samir: Yes, it's the complement to max_num_seqs; it limits aggregate token count in a micro-batch to avoid memory/latency cliffs. For example, set max_tokens_per_batch to 8192 for 13B on A100 with q4. If a batch would exceed it we split. That prevents a single long request from monopolizing a GPU.
[05:12] Danielle: So practical tuning path?
[05:15] Samir: Start with these steps: 1) Baseline current traffic with histograms (qps, tokens/request, prefix reuse). 2) Apply conservative knobs: window=10ms, max_num_seqs=16, max_tokens_per_batch=8192. 3) Run synthetic ramp to peak and measure p50/p95/p99 and GPU utilization. 4) Increase max_num_seqs or window only if p99 stays acceptable and utilization is low.
[05:36] Michael: What's an acceptable GPU utilization target?
[05:39] Samir: For A100 inference, aim 40-70% GPU SM utilization for mixed workloads; for dedicated batch jobs you can push higher but watch latency. Continuous batching often shifts utilization into that range without latency blow-up if configured.
[05:52] Aisha: Any quick wins for cost reduction?
[05:55] Samir: Yes: quantization (q4), higher packing via max_num_seqs, and prefix caching. Also route low-priority bulk jobs to cheaper spot pools and keep latency-sensitive traffic on reserved capacity.
[06:08] Owen: Are there scheduler safety limits we shouldn't cross? Like unbounded max_num_seqs?
[06:13] Priya: Don't set max_num_seqs > 128 for 13B on A100 - you'll likely hit memory/QoS issues. We enforce hard guardrails in the runtime but user-level knobs should be conservative.
[06:24] Michael: Can we see a live demo of how changing max_num_seqs affects latency distribution?
[06:29] Samir: Yes, I can show a micro-bench. (screen-share noise) Ok, I'm running a synthetic load with avg tokens 60, bursts to 200rps. Starting with max_num_seqs=8...
[06:48] [06:48] Samir: p50=64ms, p95=210ms, p99=340ms at num_seqs=8
[06:55] Samir: Increasing to 16... p50=58ms, p95=175ms, p99=310ms
[07:03] Samir: Increasing to 32... p50=62ms, p95=160ms, p99=420ms (p99 regressed due to queueing of a few long requests)
[07:12] Michael: So p95 improved but p99 worsened. That's the tradeoff we keep seeing.
[07:16] Samir: Exactly - that's why we recommend token caps or routing long requests separately. Also our scheduler has per-request priority to preempt low-priority sequences in a batch if p99 targets are violated.
[07:29] Aisha: Are preemption and priority RBAC-configurable?
[07:33] Priya: Yes, you can map priority to API keys or routes and set expedited lanes in the config. It's all in the knobs doc.
[07:41] Danielle: On telemetry - what traces/logs should we capture to debug throughput issues later?
[07:47] Samir: Capture per-request latency, queue time, batch size, num_seqs, tokens_in_batch, kv_cache_hit, GPU_util, and memory headroom. We emit these in the console and can forward to your observability stack.
[07:59] Michael: Any known transcription or naming issues with runtime logs? (laughs)
[08:02] Jordan: (laughs) Sometimes logs call KV cache kv_store or kvcache, search heuristics help.
[08:09] Samir: Back to quantization - when you move to q4, measure embed/response delta on your eval prompts. If you see >1-2% metric drift you might need to switch to hybrid q4/q8 for sensitive routes.
[08:21] Michael: Hybrid profiles? Can we mix quant levels per route?
[08:24] Samir: Yes, route-level model variants allowed. You can have q4 variant for cheap bulk, q8 for customer-facing pipeline. Runtime supports automatic fallback if q4 node pool is saturated.
[08:35] Aisha: For our Dedicated deployment in VPC, who handles KMS? We want to manage keys.
[08:40] Priya: In Private mode customers can bring-your-own KMS/HSM. We integrate with your KMS for model keys and audit logs. We'll share the KMS integration guide.
[08:50] Owen: Any perf hit for running in VPC/private vs hosted?
[08:54] Samir: Not inherently. The main differences are network latency and throughput in your VPC; if you colocate compute and storage and avoid NAT bottlenecks performance is comparable. Some overhead for control-plane checks but negligible for inference.
[09:07] Danielle: Would you recommend separate node pools for streaming vs batch?
[09:11] Samir: Yes - streaming/low-latency workloads need smaller windows and reserved capacity. Batch can be scheduled on cheaper nodes with higher max_num_seqs. It simplifies tuning and avoids interference.
[09:23] Michael: We asked about runtime scheduler knobs affecting stability - are there safety defaults that change with autoscaler?
[09:29] Priya: Autoscaler takes into account avg queue length and GPU utilization. If you push max_num_seqs high and utilization rises, autoscaler will scale up if allowed, but rapid scale-ups can cause transient scheduling delays. We recommend gradual scaling policies and burst caps.
[09:44] Jordan: Can we talk about a concrete pilot plan?
[09:47] Samir: Sure - propose: 2-week pilot on Dedicated in your VPC with 3 node pools: latency (reserved), throughput (mixed), and batch (spot). Phase 1 baseline week: measure current metrics. Phase 2 tuning week: apply knobs (window 10ms, num_seqs 16 -> 32 experiments, max_tokens_per_batch 8192), run synthetic and real traffic. Phase 3 validation: run A/B quality tests on quant profiles, evaluate cost and p99.
[10:12] Aisha: That works. We'll need pricing for Dedicated + pilot. Jordan?
[10:16] Jordan: I'll send a pilot pricing worksheet after the call, and include the SLA options.
[10:21] Michael: One more technical: what is the scheduler algorithm name? Round-robin vs packer?
[10:26] Samir: It's a workload-aware packer with latency-aware prioritization. We use a two-level scheduler: fast-packer for micro-batches and a fair-queueing front end that honors priorities and preemption hints.
[10:39] Danielle: Error modes - if we exceed memory, do you fail requests or spill to CPU?
[10:44] Samir: We fail gracefully with a retry hint; we don't spill to CPU for now. There is a soft-eviction for cold KV entries, but OOMs are fatal for the worker; autoscaler and admission control should prevent reach.
[10:57] Owen: How fast are node spin-ups? For auto-scale during a sudden burst?
[11:01] Priya: In cloud it's typically 90s-180s depending on instance type and image caching. We support warm pool mechanisms to keep spare nodes ready for faster scale. We'll include recommended warm pool sizes.
[11:12] Michael: Are there any built-in cost-prediction tools we can use?
[11:15] Jordan: Console includes token-level cost breakdowns and simulated cost projections based on traffic. We'll show an example in the pilot.
[11:22] [11:22] Samir: Quick demo: I'll flip the max_num_seqs from 16 to 24 on one node pool and watch queues. (short pause, background noise) p99 dropped from 310ms to 290ms but p95 improved to 150ms - again p99 susceptible if a few long requests slip in.
[11:45] Michael: Our logs show occasional big outliers - how to debug?
[11:48] Samir: Look for queue_time spikes, then token count per-request. If queue_time high and tokens large, you likely need token caps or routing. We can correlate with KV cache hit rate to see if prefix reuse collapsed.
[12:01] Aisha: Security/regulatory - can your audit logs be ingested into our SIEM?
[12:05] Jordan: Yes, we export structured audit logs (Cloud Audit format) and can stream to your SIEM or GCS/S3. We'll share the schema.
[12:12] Danielle: Any recommended defaults for health-check thresholds?
[12:15] Priya: Health-checks: 1) readiness should include runtime memory headroom, 2) health-check intervals around 10s and failure threshold 3, adjust as needed. Avoid aggressive health checks that trigger flaps during short GC or checkpoint ops.
[12:31] Michael: Network egress - we want to avoid over-provisioned NAT costs, you mentioned internal LB earlier - can you provide a diagram?
[12:36] Jordan: We'll share architecture diagrams. For minimal egress keep traffic internal and use private endpoints for control-plane calls.
[12:44] Aisha: Final question on rollout safety - how does canary rollback work with cached KV state?
[12:49] Samir: Good point. Canary nodes have separate KV caches; when rolling back you ensure sticky routing so the cache differences don't corrupt conversations. We recommend short TTLs for ephemeral caches during canary phases.
[13:03] Jordan: OK, we're about 40 minutes in - we'll wrap with recap and next steps.
[13:07] Jordan: Recap: share scheduler knobs doc + sample configs, quantization guidance and perf micro-benchmarks, VPC checklist, and pilot pricing. Customer to share traffic patterns and run pilot 2-week plan. Action items assigned in the doc (Samir, Michael, Priya).
[13:24] Michael: Thanks everyone - we'll get the traffic profiles to you by EOD Tuesday.
[13:29] Aisha: Appreciate the thoroughness.
[13:32] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and create the pilot Jira.
[13:36] [Call ends]
